binders: A type Ω equipped with a measurable-space structure.
A sequence X indexed by natural numbers, where each X i is a real-valued function on Ω.
hypotheses: The random variable X 0 is integrable with respect to μ.
The family X is pairwise independent with respect to μ: for every distinct natural numbers i and j, X i and X j are independent.
For every natural number i, X i and X 0 are identically distributed under μ.
conclusions: For μ-almost every ω, the sequence n ↦ (∑ i in {0, ..., n-1}, X i(ω)) / n converges as n tends to infinity to ∫ X 0 dμ.
mathematical_definitions: The nth partial sum is S_n(ω) = ∑_{i=0}^{n-1} X_i(ω).
The nth normalized partial sum is S_n(ω) / n, with n interpreted as a real number.
Pairwise independence means that X_i and X_j are independent whenever i ≠ j.
Identical distribution is taken with respect to μ on both copies of the sample space.
Almost-everywhere convergence means that the set of ω for which convergence fails has μ-measure zero.
translation.proposition_plain_english: Let X_0, X_1, ... be real-valued functions on a measurable space with measure μ. If X_0 is integrable, the functions are pairwise independent under μ, and every X_i has the same distribution as X_0 under μ, then for μ-almost every sample point ω, the averages (X_0(ω) + ... + X_{n-1}(ω)) / n converge to the integral of X_0 with respect to μ.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The measure μ is quantified as an arbitrary measure; the target does not explicitly assume that μ is a probability measure.
The normalized expression is defined at n = 0 using real division by zero, but Tendsto atTop is insensitive to finitely many initial terms.
Only pairwise independence is assumed, not mutual or joint independence of every finite subfamily.
Integrability is stated explicitly only for X 0; any corresponding regularity of X i must come through the identical-distribution hypotheses.
If the almost-everywhere filter is degenerate, for example for the zero measure, the almost-everywhere conclusion can hold vacuously.
The limiting quantity is the unnormalized integral ∫ X 0 dμ rather than division by μ(Ω), so for a non-probability finite measure it is not the usual normalized mean.
ambiguities: The packet does not state whether the definitions of IndepFun or IdentDistrib themselves force μ to have probability-measure properties.
The intended probabilistic reading appears to be a strong law of large numbers, but the formal binder exposes only a general Measure rather than an explicit probability-measure instance.

The behavior and consistency of independence and identical-distribution hypotheses for arbitrary non-probability measures cannot be determined solely from the displayed one-level dependency boundaries.
